title: Round 8: Tell the story of a production incident you owned
description: Learn to narrate a production incident in a way that shows accountability, technical depth, and a commitment to prevention rather than blame.

data.text: This round is as much about communication as it is about engineering. The interviewer asks you to describe a production incident you owned end to end. They want to know how you detected it, how you responded, and how you prevented it from happening again.

items: Situation: Describe the system and the baseline health before the incident.
Task: Explain your role and what you were responsible for during the incident.
Action: Walk through the concrete steps you took to detect, mitigate, and resolve the issue.
Result: Share the measurable outcome, such as reduced error rate or improved recovery time.
Learning: Describe the permanent changes you made to process, monitoring, or architecture.

terms.definition: Mean time to recover: the average time it takes to restore service after an incident.
A retrospective analysis that focuses on system and process improvements rather than individual fault-finding.
A documented set of procedures for responding to a specific alert or incident scenario.
The person responsible for coordinating the response, assigning roles, and making real-time decisions during an incident.

data.text: A common mistake is to tell a war story without showing personal accountability. Avoid phrases like 'the server crashed' without explaining why. Instead, say 'a memory leak in the image processing service caused an out-of-memory kill after forty-eight hours of sustained traffic.'

data.title: Brief incident timeline
data.content: Example of a concise, factual incident narrative:
data.code:
Situation: Our checkout API was returning 500 errors for 3% of requests.
Task: I was the on-call engineer for the payments domain.
Action: I checked Datadog dashboards and saw a database deadlock spike after a schema migration. I rolled back the migration, verified the error rate dropped, and then added a canary step to the deployment pipeline.
Result: Error rate returned to baseline within twelve minutes.
Learning: Schema migrations now run in a separate release pipeline with automatic rollback on deadlock detection.

data.text: How you communicate during an incident is as important as what you do. A good incident commander sends regular updates to stakeholders, assigns clear roles, and knows when to escalate. A poor response leaves customers in the dark and engineers working at cross purposes.

data.title: Communication checklist
items: Send an initial acknowledgment within 5 minutes of the alert
Update stakeholders every 15-30 minutes with status and ETA
Assign roles: incident commander, communications lead, technical lead
Use a shared incident document or Slack channel for real-time notes
After resolution, send a customer-facing postmortem summary
Did you own the detection, or did you wait for a customer to report it?
Did you coordinate with other teams or try to fix it alone?
Did you prioritize speed over safety, or did you assess impact before acting?
Did you turn the incident into a permanent process improvement?

cards.title: SEV-1 Critical
cards.description: Major customer impact or data loss. All hands on deck.

cards.title: SEV-2 High
cards.description: Degraded experience for a subset of users. Core functionality intact.

cards.title: SEV-3 Medium
cards.description: Minor impact, workaround available. Scheduled fix.

data.title: Avoid the blame game
data.text: Never blame another team or a single person. The story should be about systems and processes. If you mention a human action, frame it as a missing safeguard rather than a mistake. 'We did not have a guardrail for memory growth' is stronger than 'DevOps misconfigured the server.'

data.caption: Production incident lifecycle from detection to postmortem
data.definition:
graph TD
    A[Alert fires] --> B[On-call acknowledges]
    B --> C{Impact assessment}
    C -->|SEV-1| D[War room: all teams]
    C -->|SEV-2| E[Incident commander assigned]
    C -->|SEV-3| F[Owner investigates during business hours]
    D --> G[Mitigate: rollback, feature flag, traffic shift]
    E --> G
    F --> G
    G --> H[Verify recovery]
    H --> I[Customer communication]
    I --> J[Postmortem within 48 hours]
    J --> K[Action items assigned]
    K --> L[Follow up on fixes in next sprint]

items: Document the timeline with timestamps from logs and monitoring, not from memory.
Assign action items to specific owners with due dates.
Share the postmortem broadly, including customer-facing teams.
Revisit the action items in the next sprint planning to ensure they are completed.
Practice the incident response with game days so the team performs well under real pressure.

data.title: Write a blameless postmortem
data.description: Choose a minor incident from your past or invent a realistic scenario. Write a one-page postmortem with timeline, impact, root cause, and action items.
steps: Write the timeline using only observable data
State the user impact in numbers
Identify the root cause using the five whys or a fishbone diagram
List three action items with owners and due dates
Review for blaming language and rewrite any sentence that names a person instead of a process
data.expectedOutcome: You should produce a postmortem that focuses on system improvements and is suitable for sharing with the entire engineering organization.

data.title: Summary
points: Use STAR-L to keep the story structured
Focus on facts, metrics, and your concrete actions
Show how you turned the incident into a permanent improvement
Keep the tone accountable and forward-looking
data.takeaway: A great incident story proves that you remain calm under pressure, learn from failure, and make the system stronger for the next team.
